title: Freelance Invoicing Software in France for 2026: An Honest Guide
excerpt: A practical comparison of Freebe, Indy, Shine, Pennylane, Dougs and Qonto, plus the French e-invoicing deadlines that freelancers and small businesses need to understand.
content:
# Freelance Invoicing Software in France for 2026: An Honest Guide

This guide is written for freelancers and small businesses operating in France. It compares the main French invoicing and accounting products and explains the national e-invoicing reform. The regulatory dates and PDP requirements below are specific to France.

Have you already spent two hours comparing Pennylane, Indy, Freebe and Dougs on websites that all conclude that ‘it depends on your needs’? This guide takes a clearer position. The right choice depends mainly on your legal structure, whether you need a professional bank account and how closely you work with an accountant. ## What Changes in September 2026 French electronic invoicing requirements arrive in two stages: - **1 September 2026:** all businesses, including small companies and VAT-registered freelancers, must be able to receive electronic invoices through an approved platform. - **1 September 2027:** the obligation to issue electronic invoices extends to small businesses, SMEs and micro-entrepreneurs. If you work with large companies or mid-sized businesses, they may require your invoices in the correct electronic format from 2026. Before subscribing, ask each provider whether it is approved as a PDP or works with an approved PDP, and request a concrete compliance timetable. ## The Honest Comparison ### Freebe: Built Specifically for Freelancers **Typical price:** €9 to €15 per month. Freebe makes quotes and invoices quick to create, keeps payment tracking clear and supports URSSAF workflows for micro-entrepreneurs. It is a strong fit for solo freelancers who need straightforward invoicing. Its cash-flow view is basic, and businesses operating as SAS or SASU can outgrow it. Its bank integration is also less extensive than some competitors. **Best for:** solo freelancers, micro-entrepreneurs and simple invoicing. ### Indy: Free Invoicing with Automated Accounting Options **Typical price:** the invoicing module is free and unlimited. Paid accounting starts around €25 per month. Indy combines solid bank synchronisation with automated accounting for BNC professionals, including VAT and tax-return workflows. It is optimised for independent professionals and micro-entrepreneurs rather than every company structure. **Best for:** BNC freelancers and independent professionals who want affordable accounting automation. [View Indy on ToolTrim →](/en/tool/indy) ### Shine: Professional Banking and Invoicing in One Flow **Typical price:** invoicing is included with eligible plans. Shine is attractive when the real need is to connect a professional account, quotes, invoices, reminders and receipts. Its included invoicing can prevent an early subscription to a separate product. It is less useful if you already use Qonto, Pennylane or an accountant-imposed workflow. **Best for:** freelancers, micro-entrepreneurs and small French businesses that want banking and invoicing together. [View Shine on ToolTrim →](/en/tool/shine) ### Pennylane: Strong Collaboration with an Accountant **Typical price:** from approximately €37 per month. Pennylane provides real-time accountant collaboration and a strong cash-flow view for small businesses with multiple customers and denser financial operations. It is often presented as a universal freelance solution, but a solo freelancer issuing ten invoices a month may pay for capabilities they do not use. **Best for:** structured small businesses and founders working closely with an accountant. [View Pennylane on ToolTrim →](/en/tool/pennylane) ### Dougs: Software and Accounting Firm Combined **Typical price:** from approximately €49 per month. Dougs combines software with human accounting support. For a growing SASU, it can cost less than a traditional accounting firm. For a new freelancer, €49 to €80 a month is substantial. It is a product for delegating accounting rather than merely starting to invoice. **Best for:** growing SASU or SAS businesses and founders who want to delegate accounting. ### Qonto: Often Enough for Existing Customers **Typical price:** the invoicing module is included with the banking subscription. If Qonto is already your professional account, its integrated invoicing is sufficient for many freelancers issuing fewer than 15 to 20 invoices a month. Paying for an additional basic invoicing product may create an unnecessary duplicate. **Best for:** existing Qonto customers with moderate and straightforward invoicing. [View Qonto on ToolTrim →](/en/tool/qonto) ## Which Product Fits Which Profile? | Profile | Recommended product | Why | |---|---|---| | Micro-entrepreneur | Freebe, Indy or Shine | Simple invoicing; Shine if you also need the professional account | | BNC independent professional | Indy | Automated accounting and VAT workflows | | Active SASU freelancer | Pennylane or Dougs | More complete accounting oversight | | Small business with 2 to 10 employees | Pennylane | Cash-flow visibility and accountant collaboration | | Small business wanting full delegation | Dougs | Combined software and accounting service | | Professional account plus invoices | Shine or Qonto | Avoid duplicating banking and invoicing subscriptions | ## Three Questions to Ask Before Subscribing ### 1. Is the Product Ready for the 2026–2027 French Reform? Ask whether the provider is an approved PDP or a partner of an approved platform. A vague answer without a dated commitment is a warning sign. ### 2. Does It Connect to My Professional Bank Account? Manual transaction entry should not be necessary in 2026. Check the supported-bank list before committing, because coverage differs between providers. ### 3. What Is the Real 12-Month Cost? Some products charge extra for automated reminders, accountant access or archived-invoice storage. Calculate the price using the capabilities you will actually need. ## ToolTrim Verdict For a French micro-entrepreneur who only needs invoices, start with Indy’s free invoicing or Freebe. Choose Shine when professional banking is part of the same decision. For a SASU or a more structured business working with an accountant, Pennylane or Dougs is usually more coherent. Existing Qonto customers should test the included module before adding another subscription. The most important 2026 criterion is not the longest feature list. It is a credible and documented path to compliance with France’s electronic-invoicing reform. Verify the current PDP status directly with the provider before committing to an annual plan. *Published 8 May 2026. Sources referenced by the French edition: economie.gouv.fr, Cegid and portail-autoentrepreneur.fr.*

title: Top 5 AI Skills for Freelancers to Learn in 2026 (High-Income Skills)
excerpt: The five AI skills that separate a freelancer charging €400 a day from one charging €1,500 a day in 2026. Minimal stack, learning order and an honest ToolTrim verdict.
content:
**ToolTrim verdict:** I’ll be direct. In 2026, AI tools are no longer what separates a struggling freelancer from one who charges well. Everyone has ChatGPT and everyone experiments with Midjourney. What really changes the outcome are **five specific AI skills** that repeatedly appear among freelancers charging more than €800 a day. Here they are, the order in which to learn them and the stack you need for less than €60 a month.

I am writing this after more than 2,500 freelance-stack audits on ToolTrim. This is the advice I would give a freelance friend over coffee: what genuinely works, what is LinkedIn nonsense and what I wish someone had told me before I burned €600 on AI subscriptions ‘just to try them’.

---

## 1. AI-Augmented Research

**Why start here:** it is the least glamorous skill, but it changes everything. A freelancer who can extract in 30 minutes what competitors need two days to compile can charge the same price with four times the margin.

**In practice, you learn to:**
- Map a competitive market with one well-designed prompt
- Digest 200-page reports and extract ten actionable insights
- Conduct sourced research with citations, essential when selling B2B
- Build personas and jobs-to-be-done from real customer reviews rather than imagination

**Honest stack (€30/month):**
- **Perplexity Pro:** €10/month for sourced research and Deep Research
- **Claude Pro:** €20/month for long PDFs and its 200K-token context window

**What to avoid:** paying for ChatGPT Plus on top of Claude Pro solely for research. It is the number-one duplicate in ToolTrim audits. Forty-one percent of the freelance consultants audited pay for both without being able to explain what one does that the other cannot.

[Compare Perplexity and ChatGPT Search →](/en/guides)

> Key point: AI-augmented research is the foundation. A freelancer who extracts insights in 30 minutes when a competitor needs two days can charge the same price with four times the margin.

---

## 2. AI-Assisted Web Design and Development

**Why it pays:** a brochure website that took two weeks and sold for €4,000 in 2023 can be delivered in two days in 2026, at the same client price. You can calculate the effective day rate.

**What you will be able to do:**
- Generate a complete AI no-code website from a client brief
- Redesign a landing page with an integrated A/B test
- Connect APIs and automations without touching the backend
- Maintain a site, including debugging, refactoring and accessibility, without losing the day

**Honest stack (€45/month):**
- **Lovable:** €25/month for full-stack React and Supabase generation
- **Bolt.new:** €20/month for very fast prototyping at the start of an engagement
- **Vercel:** free until the professional threshold, which you are unlikely to reach immediately

**The truth nobody mentions:** selling an ‘AI website’ without understanding deployment, technical SEO and performance is asking for trouble. The client is not paying you for prompting Lovable. They are paying for a site that converts, gets indexed and loads in under two seconds. That is the marketable skill.

[See the No-Code App Builder stack →](/en/stacks/nocode-app-builder)

---

## 3. AI-Powered UGC Creation

**Why it pays:** DTC brands pay between €200 and €800 per UGC video. Producing ten a week with a well-tuned AI stack can create €5,000 a month as a side project. This is not a LinkedIn fantasy; three freelancers audited by ToolTrim do exactly that.

**What you will learn:**
- Credible video avatars with HeyGen or Synthesia
- Multilingual cloned voice-overs with ElevenLabs
- Automated editing optimised for TikTok, Reels and Shorts
- Clean product visuals with Midjourney or Krea AI
- UGC scripts that convert: hook, proof and CTA

**Honest stack (€55/month):**
- **HeyGen** or **Synthesia:** €25/month, not both
- **ElevenLabs:** €20/month
- **CapCut Pro:** €10/month for editing

**The common trap:** buying four video generators ‘to compare them’. You will never compare them seriously. Pick one, force yourself to master it for two months and only then judge it.

[See the AI Visual Aggregator stack →](/en/stacks/ai-visual-aggregator)

---

## 4. AI Funnel Building

**Why it ranks highly:** an automated marketing funnel that runs around the clock changes your business model. You move from billing by the hour, where time sets the ceiling, towards semi-passive revenue. It can change your freelance business, not merely your day rate.

**What it covers:**
- Funnel design from lead magnet to email sequence and sale
- Cross-tool automation with Zapier, Make or n8n depending on budget
- AI email marketing using structured sequences rather than low-quality spam
- Lead scoring and behavioural segmentation
- Qualification chatbots with Voiceflow or ManyChat

**Honest stack (€50/month):**
- **Make** or **n8n Cloud:** €20/month
- **Brevo** or **MailerLite:** €15/month
- **ChatGPT Plus:** €20/month for writing sequences

**The trap:** overspending on €150-a-month all-in-one products such as ClickFunnels when three lightweight tools deliver the same result for a third of the price. I made that mistake. Do not repeat it.

[Compare Zapier, Make and n8n →](/en/guide/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n-2026-automatiser-stack)

---

## 5. AI CRO: AI-Assisted Conversion Rate Optimisation

**Why it comes last:** this is the highest-paid freelance skill in the market in 2026, with observed average day rates of €900 to €1,500. It is also the most demanding. You cannot do it seriously without prior marketing experience.

**What you learn:**
- Read heatmaps and session recordings without inventing conclusions
- Launch fast A/B tests with AI-generated variants
- Audit a funnel and locate leaks in minutes
- Personalise landing pages for different visitors
- Run predictive analysis without pretending to be a data scientist

**Honest stack (€60/month):**
- **PostHog:** €20/month for analytics, session replay and feature flags
- **Hotjar** or an equivalent: €20/month for heatmaps
- **ChatGPT Plus:** €20/month for qualitative analysis of customer feedback

**The real differentiator:** turning data into business hypotheses rather than merely producing a list of anomalies. That is exactly what clients pay a premium for.

[See the Product Analytics stack →](/en/stacks/product-analytics-aggregator)

---

> Key point: you do not need all five skills at once. Choose two that fit your current profession, pay for no more than two tools and reach €5,000 in recurring monthly revenue before adding the third.

## In What Order Should You Learn Them?

If you are starting in 2026, this is the order that works according to ToolTrim audits:

1. **AI Research** (one month): the foundation. Without it, everything else remains superficial.
2. **AI Web Building** (two months): the fastest to monetise. Landing initial clients within 60 days is realistic.
3. **AI Funnel Building** (two months): first for your own business, then as a service.
4. **AI UGC Creation** (one month): a creative module that is faster to learn if you already have a visual eye.
5. **AI CRO** (three months): the most demanding and the best paid, so keep it for the end.

**Allow nine months to move from a conventional freelancer to an AI full-stack freelancer able to charge €1,000 or more per day.** That is a long time, and it should be. Anyone promising the same result in 30 days is selling a course, not teaching a profession.

---

## The Complete Stack If You Want Everything

| Tool | Skill | Price/month |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Pro | Research, writing | €20 |
| Perplexity Pro | Sourced research | €10 |
| Lovable | Web building | €25 |
| HeyGen | Video UGC | €25 |
| ElevenLabs | AI voice | €20 |
| Make | Automations | €20 |
| PostHog | CRO analytics | €20 |

**Gross total: €140/month.** But you genuinely do not need all five skills at once. Choose two, spend €50 to €60 a month, build your ability and upgrade when a client explicitly pays you for the third.

---

## My Freelancer-to-Freelancer Verdict

The five skills are real and profitable. But the classic 2026 trap appears three times a week in ToolTrim audits: trying to learn **all of them at once**, paying €140 a month for skills you do not yet bill for, then giving up after four months and feeling inadequate.

The strategy that works is the reverse:
1. Choose **two skills** that fit your current profession
2. Pay for **no more than two tools**, around €40 to €50 a month
3. Reach €5,000 in recurring monthly revenue with those two skills
4. Only then add the third

> *In ToolTrim audits, 78% of freelancers who attempt all five skills at once give up within four months. Those who master two thoroughly double their day rate within nine months. It is that simple.*

title: Building a Digital Product from the Field
excerpt: Nora Bensaïd designs a coordination tool alongside the healthcare workers who will actually use it.
content:
# Building a Digital Product from the Field > ‘A screen can be perfectly logical in the office and become impossible the moment its user also has to look at someone, answer the phone and remember three things.’ @ Nora Bensaïd, independent product developer ![Nora Bensaïd reviews a prototype with a coordinating nurse](/editorial/stories/nora-sante/hero.jpg)

The best products do not simplify a mock-up. They simplify a real moment, with its interruptions, constraints and responsibilities that cannot be automated.

## The Button Worked Perfectly The prototype could transmit information in three actions. Nora Bensaïd had tested it on several phones, with a slow connection and incomplete data. Yet at the health centre, the coordinating nurse cannot find the third action. She is holding a tablet, answering a colleague in the corridor and looking for the next record. The button is visible. The moment to look at it is not. Nora closes her computer and asks to repeat the sequence from the beginning. ## The Brief Described a Screen, Not a Day The project, called Relais, is intended to help several practices share the necessary information between two visits. The brief talks about a form, a status and a notification. In the field, Nora discovers work made up of temporary notes, deferred decisions and information that cannot all be handled with the same urgency. Another notification would not reduce the noise. It would move it elsewhere. > ‘Nora did not ask us which feature we wanted. She asked which mistake we were trying to prevent.’ @ Sophie Martin, coordinating nurse ## Observing Without Turning Every Action into a Requirement Nora conducts interviews in Dovetail and connects every observation to the precise moment when it appears. She does not create a feature for every irritation. She distinguishes structural constraints, local habits and workarounds that reveal a genuine gap in the system. This distinction prevents the team from digitising problems that should be solved differently. ![Nora observes the handoff between a round and the patient-record update](/editorial/stories/nora-sante/terrain.jpg) ## A Stack That Brings the Field Closer to the Code Each tool preserves a different trace of the product. None replaces conversation with the people concerned.

01

Understand

Dovetail connects observations to real risks. Decisions begin with situations, not isolated requests.

Dovetail

02

Test

Figma tests pace and priorities. Prototypes are used standing up, while interrupted and sometimes offline.

Figma

03

Build

GitHub and Storybook keep behaviour visible. Linear connects every delivery to a documented product decision.

GitHub · Storybook · Linear

04

Learn

Sentry reveals technical failures. PostHog shows abandonment without claiming to explain on its own why it happens.

Sentry · PostHog

## The First Version Does Less Nora removes free-form comments, complex tables and several status levels. Relais keeps three actions: flag, accept and hand over. Details remain available, but the next decision appears before the history. The product no longer asks the coordinator to reconstruct the priority every time she opens it. > ‘We did not make the work simpler. We made visible what had to be decided now.’ @ Nora Bensaïd ## Artificial Intelligence Stays Behind the Scenes Claude helps Nora compare reports, identify contradictions and prepare test scenarios. It never automatically summarises a clinical situation and presents it as truth. Suggestions are used during design, with human review. Inside the product, every sensitive piece of information retains its author, time and context. Nora prefers a clear absence to a plausible answer. ## Measuring Without Monitoring People PostHog tracks the time needed to complete a handoff and where the journey is abandoned. Sentry connects errors to the technical conditions that cause them. Nora does not measure the individual speed of healthcare workers. She measures the product’s ability to return information at the right moment. When the abandonment rate falls, she returns to the field. A statistical improvement can also mean that people have found a new workaround. ## The Product Begins After Delivery Relais is deployed in three practices. Every week, Nora reviews incidents, requests and observations with Sophie. Some changes enter Linear. Others become a procedure change or a short training session. Code is only part of the answer. > ‘Nora delivered a tool, but above all a way to keep questioning it without starting again from scratch.’ @ Sophie Martin ## Building Close to the Consequences Nora keeps one rule for future projects: the more consequences a digital decision creates in the real world, the closer its design must remain to those who bear them. The stack accelerates research, prototyping, development and observation. It does not replace the judgement that connects those stages. The product becomes dependable when that continuity remains visible. [Discover a field-centred product stack in ToolTrim →](/en/ma-stack)

title: Bringing Clarity Back to a Company Growing Too Fast
excerpt: Marc Delmas helps a small manufacturer regain a shared rhythm without turning every action into a procedure.
content:
# Bringing Clarity Back to a Company Growing Too Fast > ‘A company does not become disorganised because people work badly. It happens when everyone has to rebuild the context before they can act.’ @ Marc Delmas, operations consultant ![Marc Delmas and Élise Garnier review the production schedule](/editorial/stories/marc-operations/hero.jpg)

Growth brings more orders, customers and possibilities. It also creates invisible handoffs where information can be lost, delayed or change meaning.

## At Eight O’Clock, Everyone Knows What to Do By ten past eight, the workshop already smells of coffee and damp cardboard. Élise Garnier runs Lisière, a small condiment manufacturer near Angers. Twelve people prepare, package and ship short production runs for delicatessens and restaurants. The day looks organised. The schedule is displayed, orders are printed and everyone knows their station. Yet three people are waiting for the same confirmation: should the hotel batch be packaged before the wholesaler’s? The answer exists in a message sent the previous evening. Nobody knows that it has become a decision. Marc Delmas does not begin by proposing software. He asks to follow one order from the first sales conversation to the parcel leaving the building. ## Growth Had Multiplied the Versions of the Truth At Lisière, sales live in Pipedrive, production in several Google Sheets and purchasing in Élise’s inbox. Urgent problems arrive through WhatsApp. Important procedures are explained verbally, often by the person who knows them best. None of the tools is unreasonable. It is the way they fit together that forces the team to keep checking whether information is still valid. Marc photographs the boards, listens to operators and notes every moment when someone says a variation of ‘I would rather ask first’. > ‘We thought we had a discipline problem. Marc showed us that the real issue was how decisions moved between people.’ @ Élise Garnier, founder of Lisière ## Mapping the Work as It Really Happens For two days, Marc builds the flow in Miro with the people who carry it out. He separates what triggers an action, what requires a decision and what exists only as a record. The result is not a perfect diagram. It is a map of hesitation: the approved quote that does not always open a production run, the quantity change that never reaches the workshop, the quality check that remains in a notebook. ![Marc and Élise move workflow steps around directly in the workshop](/editorial/stories/marc-operations/cartographie.jpg) ## A Stack That Follows the Order Marc’s system keeps the useful tools and gives each one a precise role.

01

Sell

Pipedrive holds the commercial relationship. A won deal becomes a visible commitment, not a message someone must re-enter.

Pipedrive

02

Orchestrate

Airtable brings together orders, production runs, materials and dates. Each view serves a specific role.

Airtable

03

Connect

Make carries safe changes between systems. Exceptions remain human decisions.

Make

04

Transfer Knowledge

Process Street structures sensitive checks. Loom explains actions that still require context.

Process Street · Loom

## Automating Only What Is Already Understood Marc refuses to automate a step until two people can explain in the same way what should happen. Make now creates a production run when an order meets the right conditions. It flags quantity changes and prepares shipping information. It never chooses the priority between two customers, approves a non-conformity or changes a promised date. > ‘A useful automation removes duplicate entry. A bad automation removes the moment when someone should have stopped to think.’ @ Marc Delmas ## The Dashboard Becomes a Conversation Metabase brings together four indicators: late orders, blocked production runs, likely shortages and time spent on rework. Marc deliberately limits the dashboard. A metric that changes no decision does not belong there. Every Monday, the team spends twenty minutes reviewing these four signals. They no longer look for whoever owns the latest version. They discuss what is preventing the work from moving forward. Élise keeps an overview without becoming the compulsory route for every decision again. ## What Marc Deliberately Leaves Imperfect Some requests still arrive by phone. Operators sometimes annotate a paper document. An experienced person can change the order of a production run when they spot a risk the system cannot see. Marc is not trying to eliminate these exceptions. He wants them to become visible and capable of improving the shared way of working. The system is structured enough to pass on. It remains open enough to learn. ## Becoming One Company Again Three months later, Lisière handles more orders with the same team. Yet the most important gain is not measured in volume. Decisions no longer depend on the memory of whoever happened to be present. The tools no longer tell four competing stories. They form a path that everyone can follow, challenge and improve. > ‘I no longer spend my days redistributing information. I can finally look at where the company needs to go.’ @ Élise Garnier [See how to map an operational stack in ToolTrim →](/en/ma-stack)

title: Drawing What the Visitor Feels Before What They Look At
excerpt: Atelier Hors-Champ turns an exhibition narrative into circulation, light, and material: without mistaking a beautiful image for a well-conceived space.
content:
# Drawing What the Visitor Feels Before What They Look At > « An exhibition does not begin in front of an object. It begins the moment the body slows down, hesitates, or chooses a passage. » @ Maya Roussel, co-founder of Atelier Hors-Champ ![Two scenographers test the volumes of an exhibition under construction](/editorial/stories/atelier-hors-champ/hero.jpg)

Scenography does not fill a room. It organizes an encounter between a narrative, objects, and bodies that never all move at the same pace.

## The wall wasn't built yet, but it was already blocking the way In the vast empty hall, there is only a roll of blue masking tape, two sawhorses, and a line marked on the floor. Maya Roussel stops three metres from the entrance. She looks at the angle a plywood partition will soon form, then asks the team to move it forty centimetres. On the plan, the circulation worked. In the room, it forced the visitor to discover the first work too early, almost from the side. The wall doesn't exist yet, but the error is already perceptible. Atelier Hors-Champ is preparing **Invisible Currents**, a temporary exhibition dedicated to landscapes transformed by water. The brief brings together photographs, maps, sound fragments, and several fragile objects. The studio must give them continuity without building a set that obscures them. ## The brief spoke of content. The studio looks for a rhythm. The first meeting produced a list: forty-two pieces, seven filmed interviews, three listening installations, and a route accessible in under fifty minutes. Maya doesn't immediately translate this list into hanging surfaces. With Idriss, architect-scenographer, she maps the shifts in density: where does the visitor need to understand, where can they simply feel, where should the gaze rest? They divide the route into five intensities rather than five themes. A narrow room brings the voices closer. A low passageway slows the body. A full-height opening restores distance before the final works. > « The client entrusts us with content. Our responsibility is to build the conditions in which it can be received. » @ Maya Roussel ## Drawing at the scale of the body Plans become more precise. The model contradicts them. On a black table, the team moves fragments of grey cardboard, slides a scaled silhouette between two panels, and photographs each variation at eye level. A curve that seemed generous on screen becomes overbearing in volume. A threshold designed as a moment to breathe looks like an exit. The model doesn't illustrate a solution: it forces the team to question it before the timber is ordered. [[story-gallery]] ![The team's hands reposition the volumes of a physical model](/editorial/stories/atelier-hors-champ/maquette.jpg) ![A plywood joint is painted during the install](/editorial/stories/atelier-hors-champ/montage.jpg) [[/story-gallery]] ## A stack that scales with the project The studio doesn't look for a single tool. It organizes a clean handoff between reference, space, approval, and site work.

01

Collect

Are.na holds the visual references. Notion gathers the brief, the constraints, and the decisions that must not get lost in the images.

Are.na · Notion

02

Test

Rhino checks volumes and sight lines. The physical model brings every hypothesis to the scale of a real body.

Rhino · Physical model

03

Get sign-off

Frame.io concentrates feedback on renders and films. Airtable links each decision to a piece, a supplier, and a deadline.

Frame.io · Airtable

04

Install

Site monitoring makes dependencies and outstanding issues visible. Unexpected problems are resolved on site, with the craftspeople.

Airtable · Slack

## Light doesn't come last A week before the install, Inès, lighting designer, sets up three projectors in a darkened studio. The team isn't looking for the right colour yet. It observes what light does to the materials: the indigo voile absorbs shadows, the light wood reflects white too strongly, a photograph disappears the moment the beam touches the polished floor. The lighting plan evolves with the route. A darker zone doesn't serve to artificially dramatize an object; it prepares the eye to perceive a low-contrast film. Elsewhere, raking light reveals the weave of a textile without displaying it as an effect. At Hors-Champ, lighting doesn't dress the scenography. It sets its punctuation. ## What the studio refuses to automate The team uses artificial intelligence to open research leads, sort meeting notes, and quickly produce variations of internal documents. It does not delegate the final form of the route, the selection of materials, or the interpretation of visitor feedback to it. A generated image can make an intention look compelling before it is even feasible to build. Maya is particularly wary of this at the start of a project: the apparent precision of a render can close a conversation that should remain open. The studio prefers an incomplete but debatable drawing to a perfect image that conceals its assumptions. ## Installation puts every decision back in its place On the third morning, an arch arrives twelve millimetres too tall. The technical sheet is correct, the survey too. It is the old floor of the hall, imperceptibly rising near the wall. The team could plane the piece down and carry on. Instead, they take twenty minutes to check the effect on the light line, the tension of the textile, and the passage of a wheelchair. The problem is never just the piece that doesn't fit. It's the chain of decisions it displaces. On site, documents stop being evidence. They become tools for deciding together. ## At the opening, the set must almost disappear ![The completed scenography combines indigo voiles, curved timber, and amber light](/editorial/stories/atelier-hors-champ/lumiere.jpg) The evening of the opening, Maya stays near the entrance. She doesn't look at the works. She watches shoulders, distances, and turnarounds. A group spontaneously clusters in the room of voices. A child walks around the arch, then comes back to take in: at a glance: the piece she had just passed. The route doesn't impose a single reading. It gives enough cues for each person to build their own without getting lost. > « Our work succeeds when the space stays present in the memory, but no one feels the need to comment on it during the visit. » @ Maya Roussel Atelier Hors-Champ rolls up its plans. In two months, the exhibition will be dismantled. The timber will move to another project, the voiles will be cut down, and the hall will find its emptiness again. The scenography is temporary. The attention it organized can last considerably longer. [Build a creative stack that respects the way you work →](/fr/ma-stack)

title: Auditing Your SaaS Stack in 45 Minutes: Removing Overlaps Without Breaking Your Workflow
excerpt: A practical method to determine which tools to keep, challenge, replace, or remove: taking cost, real-world usage, and migration risk into account.
content:
# Auditing Your SaaS Stack in 45 Minutes: Removing Overlaps Without Breaking Your Workflow

A stack rarely becomes cluttered in a single decision. It accumulates gradually: a tool added for a client, a trial that became a paid subscription, a forgotten automation, then two applications that end up solving nearly the same problem.

The goal of this audit is not to reach the shortest possible stack. It is to make every subscription legible: **what it enables, how often it is actually used, what depends on it, and why it still earns its cost**.

![A stack built up without a clear role for each tool](/editorial/stack-visuale/franken-stack-photo.jpg)

> Key takeaway: do not remove anything during the audit. The 45 minutes are meant to produce reasoned decisions, not to trigger improvised migrations.

## Before You Start: Define Your Scope

A company-wide audit can take several days. In 45 minutes, pick a single environment: your freelance practice, one team, one project, or a frequently used workflow.

Prepare three sources:

- your bank statement or subscription list;
- installed applications and browser extensions;
- your calendar from the past two weeks.

The statement shows what you pay for. The applications show what you have adopted. The calendar reflects what you actually do. No single source is sufficient on its own.

Then create one row per tool with five columns: **role, frequency, monthly cost, important data, and dependencies**. A spreadsheet is sufficient for this initial collection. The visual view comes later, when mapping relationships.

## 0–10 Minutes: Inventory Without Judging

List every service involved in your chosen scope, free and paid alike. A free tool can fragment your work just as much as an expensive subscription.

Do not try yet to decide whether to keep it. Simply note:

- the amount actually charged, taxes included;
- the plan in use;
- the renewal date;
- the account owner;
- whether an export or backup option exists.

Add invisible tools: storage, e-signature, password managers, automation, scheduling, and add-ons. They are often missing from lists because they work silently in the background.

### The One-Sentence Test

For each row, complete this sentence: **"I use this tool to…"**

An answer like "manage my business" is too vague. "Turn an accepted lead into a scheduled project" is actionable. If two tools receive the same sentence, you have found an overlap worth examining: not yet a confirmed duplicate.

## 10–20 Minutes: Assign a Real Role

Map each tool to a step in your actual workflow rather than a marketing category. For example: capture a request, decide, produce, get approval, deliver, invoice, or archive.

![Tools placed in the actual order of the workflow](/editorial/stack-visuale/workflow-photo.jpg)

This approach avoids a common trap: treating two applications as competitors when they operate at different stages. Notion can document a project while a CRM holds the commercial history. Their interfaces may look similar, but their authority is not the same.

Conversely, a task manager and a database can genuinely overlap if the same deadlines are entered in both.

### Designating a Single Source of Truth

For every important piece of information, ask where the authoritative version lives:

- the status of a lead;
- the next deadline;
- the latest version of a deliverable;
- the decision approved by the client;
- the amount to invoice.

If the answer depends on who you ask, the problem is not necessarily the number of tools. It is the absence of a rule between them.

> Key takeaway: two tools can coexist. Two sources of truth for the same decision almost always create friction.

## 20–30 Minutes: Measure Usage, Not Intention

Assign each tool an observed frequency: daily, weekly, monthly, occasional, or inactive. Use the past two weeks of actual work, not the ideal scenario you imagined when you subscribed.

Then calculate a simple indicator:

**cost per use = monthly cost / number of meaningful uses in the month**

This number does not decide on its own. A password manager can be indispensable without producing any visible deliverable. It does, however, reveal subscriptions used once a quarter when a free or one-off option would cover the need.

Finally, add the consequence of unavailability:

- **low**: a manual alternative is immediately available;
- **medium**: work slows down but remains possible;
- **high**: a delivery, a payment, or access to data would be blocked.

A rarely used but critical tool must not be treated as a forgotten subscription.

## 30–40 Minutes: Check Dependencies

Before removing a tool, map what goes in, what comes out, and what connects to it.

Check in particular:

- active automations;
- forms and public links;
- templates used by the team;
- integrations with invoicing or payment;
- files whose original exists nowhere else;
- shared access granted to clients.

A €12 subscription may look easy to cancel yet prove costly to rebuild if it triggers ten automations. Conversely, a tool presented as central may be connected to nothing and only receive copies.

### The Exit Cost

Estimate the time needed to export, clean, import, test, and communicate the change. This exit cost must be weighed against the annual savings, not just the next payment.

Cancelling a €15/month subscription saves €180 per year. If the migration takes two full days and improves no workflow, the decision can wait. If it removes a daily double-entry, the gain likely exceeds the subscription cost.

## 40–45 Minutes: Make Four Types of Decision

Every tool must leave the audit in exactly one column.

| Decision | When to use it | Next action |
|---|---|---|
| **Keep** | Clear role, real usage, acknowledged dependency | Document its function and owner |
| **Challenge** | Useful, but cost, plan, or frequency are questionable | Test a lower plan or measure usage for 30 days |
| **Replace** | Real need, but a better tool or arrangement is available | Prepare export, parallel test, and rollback plan |
| **Remove** | No distinct role, no meaningful usage, no critical dependency | Back up, then cancel on the chosen date |

Avoid a "to be decided" column. It defers exactly the decision the audit was meant to produce. When uncertain, place the tool in "Challenge" with a measurement and a date: for example, count its uses over the next thirty days.

![A visual audit that surfaces overlaps and decisions](/editorial/stack-visuale/simplifier-stack-photo.jpg)

## Illustrative Example: From €94 to €48 per Month

Consider an independent consultant using eight services. The figures below are an **illustrative assumption**, not a record of current vendor pricing.

| Tool and function | Example cost | Observation | Decision |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Document workspace | €14 | Used daily, single source of truth | Keep |
| Project management | €11 | Same tasks exist in the document workspace | Remove after export |
| Scheduling | €10 | Used every week and connected to the website | Keep |
| Async video | €15 | Two videos sent in three months | Challenge for 30 days |
| Automation | €20 | Single scenario, inactive for six weeks | Remove after verification |
| Client messaging | €8 | Required by two active clients | Keep |
| Password manager | €4 | Critical for shared access | Keep |
| Delivery storage | €12 | Contractual archive for deliverables | Keep |

This scenario immediately removes €31 in overlaps or unused automations. The async video tool is kept for one month under observation, then removed if no usage justifies its cost. The stack drops from €94 to €48 per month.

The annual saving reaches €552, but the most important result is elsewhere: tasks no longer exist in two systems, and every important piece of information has a known home.

## What Not to Remove Too Quickly

Three categories of tools require particular caution.

### Tools That Hold Client Data

Check export options, retention periods, access rights, and contractual obligations. Deleting an account is not an archiving strategy.

### Tools That Control an Identity or Payment

Primary email, domain, password manager, invoicing, and payment systems structure access to your practice. Always prepare a recovery procedure and test before switching.

### Tools Used by Someone Else

A subscription can appear unnecessary from your own perspective while remaining central to a collaborator or client. The audit is about real work, not only your own login history.

## Turning the Audit into a Monthly Rule

A one-time audit clears what already exists. An entry rule prevents clutter from returning.

Before adding a new tool, require four answers:

1. What observed problem does it solve?
2. Which tool or step does it replace?
3. What data will be authoritative there?
4. By what date will we decide to keep or cancel it?

Add a ten-minute monthly review: new subscriptions, tools with no usage, and failing automations. The goal is not to question everything every month, but to catch drift before it becomes an architecture.

## Your Deliverable After 45 Minutes

By the end, you should have:

- a complete inventory of your chosen scope;
- a precise role for each tool;
- a single source of truth for each critical piece of information;
- a dated decision for each tool;
- one priority migration, and one only.

Do not launch three replacements in parallel. Start with the decision that removes the most friction at the lowest risk, measure the result, then continue.

ToolTrim lets you gather your tools in **My Stack**, visualize their roles, and explore alternatives without losing the context of your current system.

[**Start the audit in My Stack →**](/fr/ma-stack)

[Compare tools before replacing a component →](/fr/comparatifs)

> Key takeaway: a good stack is not minimal by principle. It is explainable, under control, and simple enough that every tool justifies its place.

faq.question: How long does it take to audit a SaaS stack?
faq.answer: A focused first audit can fit into 45 minutes if you limit the scope to a single practice or workflow. A full team or company will require multiple sessions and interviews with the relevant users.

faq.question: How do you identify an overlap between two tools?
faq.answer: Two tools overlap when the same information is authoritative in both, or when the same action is maintained in parallel in each. Similar features are not enough: two tools can remain complementary if they operate at different stages.

faq.question: Should every low-usage tool be removed?
faq.answer: No. A low-frequency tool may remain critical for security, invoicing, archiving, or a contractual obligation. Frequency must be weighed against the consequence of unavailability and the exit cost.

faq.question: What is the difference between challenging and replacing a tool?
faq.answer: Challenging means measuring usage, reviewing the plan, or testing a hypothesis before deciding. Replacing means the need remains, but a different solution or arrangement has already been chosen and must be migrated cleanly.

title: Designing like a studio when you work alone
excerpt: Anna Morel builds a system where artificial intelligence handles the scattered parts: without making creative decisions in her place.
content:
# Designing like a studio when you work alone > "My work is not to produce as many images as possible. It is to know which one deserves to exist." @ Anna Morel, independent brand designer ![Anna Morel organises the visual references for a project in her Lyon studio](/editorial/stories/anna-morel/hero.jpg)

When producing becomes almost instantaneous, the designer's value shifts. It lies less in the number of directions created than in the ability to recognise the one that deserves to remain.

## A sentence stays on the table At twenty past nine, Anna Morel moves the same photograph for the third time. The morning light cuts through her Lyon studio and slices the reference wall into pale rectangles. On the table, two notebooks lie open, a client interview is still up on the screen, and several typographic explorations overlap one another. She has been working for three weeks on Sillage, a young skincare brand created by Claire Vignal. The product exists, the first customers too, but the brand still looks like every other. Claire talks about precision, silence, and passed-down gestures. Competitors say exactly the same things. Anna re-reads a sentence spoken almost in passing during their first conversation: "I don't want our customers to collect our products. I want them to know which one to keep." She prints it out and places it at the centre of the table. It is not yet a brand idea. It is a constraint strong enough to eliminate easy ideas. ## The problem was not a lack of images For a long time, Anna began each project with the feeling of having too much material and not enough context. A photograph sat in her phone. A reference found six months earlier slept in a folder. A decisive remark was lost in the middle of a fifty-page transcript. She could produce quickly, but first had to reconstruct the thread linking each element to the project. "I thought I lacked time to create," she says. "In reality, I was mostly spending my time finding again what I had already understood." Her first instinct was not to add artificial intelligence. She began by giving a precise function to each workspace. Are.na became the space for open collection: where an image can arrive before Anna even knows why it matters. Eagle then takes in the private library: photographs, typefaces, screenshots, textures, and already-qualified references. In Milanote, she no longer sorts. She brings things closer together. ![References remain deliberately mobile until a tension appears](/editorial/stories/anna-morel/matiere.jpg) ## Listening before composing For Sillage, Anna conducted four interviews: Claire, her co-founder, a formulator, and a long-standing customer. The conversations were transcribed and structured in Dovetail. Anna links the verbatims to recurring themes, but also holds onto the sentences that resist classification. Claude comes in during a second reading. She asks it to flag contradictions, words used with multiple meanings, and questions nobody answered. She never asks it to produce a concept. A tension emerges: the brand describes itself as minimalist, yet customers mostly speak of trust, repetition, and familiarity. The project must therefore not simply appear simpler. It must make the choice more obvious. > "AI doesn't give me the direction. It helps me see the places where I haven't looked closely enough yet." @ Anna Morel [[story-gallery]] ![Anna re-reads the interviews and compares the words used by different people](/editorial/stories/anna-morel/analyse.jpg) ![Signs, materials and photographs are handled before entering a file](/editorial/stories/anna-morel/matiere.jpg) [[/story-gallery]] ## A stack that follows the gestures of the craft Anna's system does not try to centralise everything. It follows the progressive transformation of raw material.

01

Observe

Are.na receives still-fragile intuitions. Eagle keeps what has been chosen. This separation avoids confusing discovery with decision.

Are.na · Eagle

02

Understand

Dovetail links interviews to project themes. Claude acts as a critical reader, never as an art director.

Dovetail · Claude

03

Compose

Milanote holds the visual territories. Krea occasionally tests a light quality, a density, or a framing.

Milanote · Krea

04

Produce

Illustrator draws the precise marks. Figma holds the brand system. Framer quickly tests an identity in context.

Illustrator · Figma · Framer

## Two directions, then a conversation Anna prepares two territories for Sillage. The first is calm, precise, and almost clinical. It perfectly translates the brief. The second is more tactile. The compositions breathe less, the photographs seem taken at hand height, and the typography more openly embraces traces of gesture. Claire looks at the first direction for a long time. "This is exactly what we asked for," she says. Then she returns to the second. In it she recognises the formulation notebooks, the workshop shelves, and the way her customers keep a product near the basin. This direction answers the brief less literally, but it resembles the company more. ![Claire Vignal confronts the two directions with Anna during a working session](/editorial/stories/anna-morel/presentation.jpg) > "Anna didn't arrive with fifty images asking us to choose. She showed us two ways of becoming more coherent, then helped us understand which one belonged to us." @ Claire Vignal, founder of Sillage ## Producing more is no longer the problem Claire's remark changes the rest of the project. Anna is no longer trying to enrich the second direction. She removes what is stopping it from being obvious. Krea can generate variations of material, light, or composition within minutes. Figma allows a system to be rolled out at a speed that would once have taken several days. Framer makes an intention interactive before the site is even built. This speed does not reduce the work of selection. It increases it. Anna therefore sets herself three rules. A generated image never goes directly into a deliverable. An important decision must be explainable without citing the tool that produced it. A proposal that could suit ten other brands returns to the exploration space. > "An image can be beautiful and completely useless. If it changes no decision, it solves nothing." @ Anna Morel ## What she refuses to automate Anna does not delegate the final selection of a direction. She does not let a tool write the presentation accompanying a concept on its own. She does not automatically turn a client comment into a task. When someone says "this lacks energy," the problem is not necessarily in the colour. It may come from the rhythm, the typography, the photography, or simply from the fear of change. Interpreting that sentence is part of the craft. She also keeps a half-day free of generation and automatic summarising at the start of each project. She re-reads the interviews, handles the references, and writes her own observations. This silence allows her to distinguish what she thinks from what the system is proposing. ## The system makes collaboration more precise Once the direction is chosen, Anna brings other people into the project. For Sillage, a photographer translates the visual principles into images. A developer confronts the system with the constraints of the future site. The files do not arrive as a fixed set of rules but as an intention clear enough to guide their decisions. ![Anna and the project photographer select the images that genuinely extend the direction](/editorial/stories/anna-morel/collaboration.jpg) Technology has not turned her practice into an autonomous studio. It has allowed her to recognise more precisely the moment when another perspective becomes necessary. In the evening, Anna closes Figma before removing several images from the wall. The sentence printed that morning remains at the centre. It was there from the first interview, hidden within several hours of conversation. The system helped her find it again. The choice to keep it is hers. > "I don't want AI to create in my place. I want it to help me stay longer with the questions that matter." @ Anna Morel ## Designing a way of working Anna's augmented studio is not measured by the number of tools she uses. It is measured by the quality of the transitions between them. A word becomes an insight. A reference becomes a direction. A direction becomes a system. The system finally becomes something other people can use without losing the original intention. It is in these transitions that her craft gains value. [Discover Anna's daily stack on ToolTrim →](/fr/ma-stack)

title: Why Visualize Your SaaS Stack Instead of Managing It in Excel
excerpt: A list inventories your subscriptions. A map reveals duplicates, blind spots, and the real path of your work. Here's how to make your stack finally readable.
content:
*"Forget ChatGPT: this new AI will cut your working time in half."*

If you're a freelancer or solopreneur, you see this promise almost every day. One click, a free trial, then one more tool joins your daily routine. Rarely your system.

After a few months, the pile starts to look like a **Franken-stack**: notes live in Apple Notes, tasks in Notion, drafts in Google Drive, and invoices in software whose password you're still hunting for.

The problem isn't just the cost of the subscriptions. **It's the mental load of an ecosystem that has become invisible.**

![Freelancer confronted with a fragmented digital stack](/editorial/stack-visuale/hero-stack-visuelle.jpg)

A spreadsheet can count your tools. It can't show you how you work. And that's precisely where the disorder begins.

## A list answers the wrong question

When a stack turns chaotic, the first instinct is reasonable: open Excel or create a Notion database with the tool name, its price, and the renewal date.

That's useful for taking stock. Not for understanding the system.

A row doesn't say **when** the tool comes into play, **what goes in**, **what comes out**, or **which tool picks up next**. It puts everything on the same level: the software used eight hours a day and the subscription forgotten for six months each occupy exactly one row.

### Three blind spots in your spreadsheet

- **Context disappears.** "Google Drive: $12" doesn't tell you whether Drive is your archive, your delivery space, or simply the drawer where files end up.
- **Dependencies stay hidden.** An idea captured in one tool, drafted in a second, then published in a third forms a journey. The spreadsheet shows only the loose parts.
- **Friction can't be counted.** Every "Wait, where did I put it?" imposes a micro-search and breaks concentration. No column truly measures that hesitation.

> Key takeaway: Excel is excellent for tracking a cost or a deadline. It falls short the moment you want to understand a workflow.

## What a visual view really changes

Visualizing your stack isn't about sticking logos onto a pretty chart. It's about representing tools **in the order and context in which they actually serve you**.

![Freelancer organizing the stages of their workflow](/editorial/stack-visuale/workflow-photo.jpg)

From there, the question is no longer "What software do I own?", but "How does my work move from one stage to the next?"

That difference seems slight. Yet it changes the decisions you're able to make.

### 1. Duplicates become obvious

Three apps built around note-taking aren't necessarily a problem. They become one when none of them has a clear role. On a map, the accumulation jumps out immediately. You can then choose: one primary app, one deliberate exception, and the rest to cut.

### 2. Gaps appear before they cost time

You can have many tools and still be missing an essential step: no reliable place to validate a deliverable, track a follow-up, or archive a client decision. An empty zone in the flow is more telling than a long, well-filled list.

### 3. Unnecessary handoffs become visible

Copying data, downloading a file, renaming it, then re-importing it elsewhere: taken individually, each action seems trivial. Strung together, the workflow reveals five tool switches for a task that should require two.

![Visual audit to remove a duplicate and clarify a step](/editorial/stack-visuale/simplifier-stack-photo.jpg)

## A good stack isn't the one with the fewest tools

Software minimalism can become just as sterile an obsession as accumulation. The goal isn't to set a record with three subscriptions.

A good stack is one where every building block has:

- a comprehensible role;
- a place within a real objective;
- a clear relationship with what comes before and after;
- a reason to stay paid.

A specialized tool can perfectly justify its place if it prevents errors or smooths out an important step. Conversely, a free tool remains costly if it scatters information and forces you to search.

## Map your stack in 15 minutes

Start small. Take a single frequent flow: for example from client request to invoice: and write down the stages rather than the software.

1. **Write the final objective.** "Deliver a validated, invoiced project" is more useful than "organize my tools."
2. **Lay out the main stages.** Capture, plan, produce, validate, deliver, invoice.
3. **Place one primary tool under each stage.** If there are three, ask which one actually has authority.
4. **Trace the handoffs.** Spot double entries, manual exports, and manual searches.
5. **Mark one single decision.** Delete a duplicate, clarify a role, or test a replacement. There's no need to rebuild your entire system in a single evening.

> Key takeaway: A useful map doesn't try to be exhaustive. It must make the next decision visible.

## Make your digital environment a real workspace

For a freelancer, the SaaS stack is the office. Ideas are stored there, deliverables are built there, and client relationships are maintained there. This space deserves more than a subscription list consulted once a quarter.

ToolTrim lets you group your tools in **My Stack**, organize them by objective, and explore alternatives or complements without losing context. The promise isn't to choose for you. It's to give you a clear enough view to decide.

[**Visualize my stack in ToolTrim →**](/fr/ma-stack)

Start with the tools you're using this week. The rest can wait.

title: How Huberman Lab Built an Audience of Over One Million Subscribers with Kit
excerpt: Case study: how Huberman Lab connected podcast, free resource, automations and recommendations in Kit to grow a direct, owned audience.
content:
# How Huberman Lab Built an Audience of Over One Million Subscribers with Kit ![A creator reviewing a podcast episode transcript in a recording studio](/editorial/guides/kit-huberman-systeme-audience/hero.jpg)

Andrew Huberman already had a substantial audience around his podcast. The challenge was turning that dispersed attention across platforms into a direct, lasting relationship. Huberman Lab chose Kit to build that bridge.

## The case study at a glance - **Company:** Huberman Lab - **Activity:** podcast and educational content around neuroscience, health and performance - **Starting point:** approximately 6,000 email subscribers - **Goal:** convert the podcast and website audience into an owned audience - **Solution:** forms, free resource, automations, welcome sequence and recommendations network in Kit - **Result reported by Kit:** over one million subscribers The figures presented in this article come from the case study published by Kit. ToolTrim analyses how the system works and the lessons applicable to creators and freelancers. ## Who is Andrew Huberman? Andrew Huberman is an American neuroscientist and the creator of **Huberman Lab**, a podcast dedicated to how the brain works, health and daily habits. Episodes are long, often heavily researched, and accompanied by resources that allow listeners to go deeper. This depth has built a loyal audience across podcast platforms, YouTube and the Huberman Lab website. But a large audience on a platform remains a borrowed audience. An algorithm change, a drop in reach or a shift in usage patterns can sever the connection with a significant portion of that public. Email was meant to allow Huberman Lab to reach its readers and listeners directly, without waiting for a platform to decide whether to show them the next piece of content. ## The challenge: turning attention into a direct relationship Huberman Lab was not short of content. The problem lay in the transition between discovering an episode and subscribing to the newsletter. Simply asking visitors to "join the list" would have been too vague. The team needed to give them an immediate reason to leave their email address, then extend that first interaction with consistent content. Three needs emerged: 1. offering a resource valuable enough to trigger a sign-up; 2. welcoming each new subscriber automatically; 3. growing the list without depending solely on new publications. The proposition is precise. The visitor is not signing up to receive unspecified news. They receive a concrete resource, directly connected to the questions that led them to the podcast or website. According to Kit, the automation associated with Daily Blueprint generated more than **580,000 subscribers**. This result highlights the importance of the link between public content and the sign-up promise. Kit facilitates delivery and tracking, but conversion starts with a resource the audience genuinely wants. ### A form accessible across the entire site Sign-ups do not depend on an isolated campaign. # AI Tips for Freelancers in 2026: Minimal Stack, Prompts That Actually Work, and Cutting the Waste

**Verdict:** In 2026, a freelancer needs **one general-purpose AI subscription** (ChatGPT Plus *or* Claude Pro, not both) plus **one role-specific tool** based on their profile. According to tooltrim.com, 62% of freelancers paying for an AI stack run ChatGPT + Claude + Perplexity + Copilot in parallel — that's $60-80/month for 3 tools doing the same 80% of the job.

This guide covers the only three things that actually matter:

1. **The minimal AI stack by profile** (dev, designer, content, consultant, ops)
2. **The prompts and workflows that genuinely save time** (real, not theoretical)
3. **The anti-waste audit** to recover $40-60/month

No "10 productivity hacks with AI". Just the concrete stuff, based on tooltrim.com audits of 2,500+ freelancers.

---

## Part 1 — The Minimal AI Stack in 2026

### The 1 + 1 rule

According to tooltrim.com, the optimal AI stack for a solo freelancer fits in **two subscriptions max**:

- **1 general-purpose AI** (ChatGPT Plus, Claude Pro, or Gemini Advanced) — $20/month
- **1 role-specific AI tool** (Cursor for dev, Midjourney for design, etc.)

**Target total: $30-50/month.**

Beyond that, you're paying for features that overlap 70-90%.

### Picking your generalist AI: the real matchup

| Criterion | ChatGPT Plus ($20) | Claude Pro ($20) | Gemini Advanced ($22) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Long-form writing | Good | **Excellent** | Good |
| Code | **Excellent** | Excellent | Decent |
| Document analysis | Good | **Excellent** (200K tokens) | Good |
| Web search | **Excellent** (built-in) | Limited | Good |
| Image generation | **Excellent** (built-in) | No | Decent |
| Voice mode | **Excellent** | No | Good |

*Prices verified by tooltrim.com on 2026-04-29.*

**Tooltrim.com verdict:**
- You write a lot (newsletters, articles, copy) → **Claude Pro**
- You code or do heavy web research → **ChatGPT Plus**
- You already live in Google Workspace → **Gemini Advanced** (native Gmail/Docs integration)

[Detailed Claude vs ChatGPT vs DeepSeek comparison →](/en/guide/claude-vs-chatgpt-deepseek)

### The AI stack by freelance profile

#### 💻 Freelance Dev — Théo

**Recommended stack ($45/month):**
- Cursor Pro — $20/month
- ChatGPT Plus — $20/month (research + debugging)
- GitHub Copilot — already covered if you have Cursor

**Avoid:** Claude Pro *on top of* ChatGPT Plus (generalist duplicate). Free Codeium *on top of* Cursor (IDE duplicate).

#### 🎨 Freelance Designer — Sofia

**Recommended stack ($40/month):**
- Midjourney — $10/month (basic plan is enough)
- Claude Pro — $20/month (briefs, mood boards, prompts)
- Runway or Krea AI — $10/month if you do video

**Avoid:** DALL-E 3 *on top of* Midjourney. Adobe Firefly *on top of* another image generator.

#### 📝 Content Creator — Alix

**Recommended stack ($30/month):**
- Claude Pro — $20/month (long-form writing, structure)
- Perplexity Pro — $10/month (sourced research)

**Avoid:** ChatGPT Plus *on top of* Claude Pro (generalist duplicate). Jasper or Copy.ai (Claude is better for 4× less).

#### 📊 Consultant — Marc

**Recommended stack ($20/month):**
- ChatGPT Plus — $20/month (covers 90% of consulting use cases: doc analysis, structuring, research)

**Avoid:** Everything else. According to tooltrim.com, a consultant on a mission rarely needs more than one generalist AI.

#### ⚡ Ops Manager — Claire

**Recommended stack ($20/month):**
- ChatGPT Plus — $20/month (light automation, process docs, data analysis)
- Notion AI — *only if* you live inside Notion (otherwise duplicates ChatGPT)

**Avoid:** Zapier AI add-ons. n8n cloud. According to tooltrim.com, ChatGPT + a text editor covers 95% of freelance ops needs.

[See all guides by profile →](/en/guides)

---

## Part 2 — The Prompts and Workflows That Actually Work

No "10 magic prompts". Here are the **5 genuinely profitable AI workflows** identified across tooltrim.com audits.

### Workflow 1 — 30-second structuring

**For who?** Every freelancer who writes (client emails, proposals, articles).

**The prompt:**

```
You're my editorial assistant. Here's a messy draft: [paste].
Restructure it into:
1. A clear hook in 1 sentence
2. 3 main points with one proof per point
3. A concrete call to action

Don't change the tone. Don't add information.
```

**Measured gain:** 15-25 minutes saved per 500-word piece. According to tooltrim.com, this is the highest-ROI workflow across all profiles.

### Workflow 2 — Client call recap

**For who?** Consultants, ops, account managers.

**Setup:**
1. Record the call (Loom, Granola, or a simple voice recorder)
2. Transcribe (free with Whisper or ChatGPT voice)
3. Prompt:

```
Here's a client call transcript. Give me:
- 3 key points discussed
- Decisions made (who does what, by when)
- Open questions to clarify
- A ready-to-send recap email

Transcript: [paste]
```

**Measured gain:** 20-40 minutes saved per 1-hour call. ROI breaks even on the second call.

### Workflow 3 — Code review (devs) or design review (designers)

**For who?** Solo devs and designers without a peer to review their work.

**Dev prompt:**

```
Review this code as a senior dev would. Look for:
- Potential bugs
- Performance issues
- Duplicated code
- Missing error handling
For each finding, give the concrete fix.

Code: [paste]
```

**Designer prompt:**

```
You're a senior product designer. Critique this UI on:
- Visual hierarchy
- Primary CTA legibility
- Design system consistency
- Accessibility (contrast, text size)
Give 3 priority fixes.

Image: [upload]
```

**Measured gain:** Saves 1 to 3 client back-and-forths per week. According to tooltrim.com, this single workflow justifies the AI subscription.

### Workflow 4 — A commercial proposal in 10 minutes

**For who?** Consultants, freelancers in pre-engagement.

**The prompt:**

```
You're my sales assistant. Here are my client brief notes: [paste].
Generate a structured proposal:
1. Understanding of the need (3 lines)
2. Proposed approach (max 3 phases)
3. Concrete deliverables per phase
4. Time and rate estimate (day rate: $[X])
5. Conditions and next steps

Style: direct, jargon-free, results-oriented.
```

**Measured gain:** 1h-1.5h per proposal. At $80/h billed, the AI pays for itself on the first proposal of the month.

### Workflow 5 — Auditing your own processes

**For who?** Every freelancer, once per quarter.

**The prompt:**

```
Here's a description of my current workflow for [recurring task]:
[describe in 5-10 lines]

Identify:
- The 2 most time-consuming steps
- What can be automated with a tool or AI
- A simplified version of this workflow
```

**Measured gain:** 1-3 hours per week if you act on the suggestions. According to tooltrim.com, this is the least-used workflow even though it's the most profitable on a yearly basis.

---

## Part 3 — The Anti-Waste AI Audit

This is where most freelancers lose $40-60/month without noticing.

### The 4 most common AI duplicates

According to tooltrim.com audits across 2,500+ freelance stacks, here are the most common useless overlaps:

| Duplicate | Frequency | Possible savings |
|---|---|---|
| ChatGPT Plus + Claude Pro | 38% | $20/month |
| ChatGPT Plus + Perplexity Pro | 27% | $10/month (use GPT search) |
| Cursor + Copilot + Codeium | 19% | $20-30/month |
| Notion AI + ChatGPT Plus | 16% | $10/month (Notion AI) |

**Average recoverable total:** $45/month or **$540/year**.

### The 3-question test

Before keeping an AI subscription, ask yourself:

1. **Do I open it at least 3 times a week?** If no → cancel.
2. **Does it do something no other tool in my stack does?** If no → cancel the less versatile one.
3. **Can I name 1 concrete task where it saved me time this week?** If no → cancel.

According to tooltrim.com, 70% of freelance AI subscriptions fail at least 2 of these 3 questions.

### "Ghost" AI subscriptions to cut

Frequently forgotten but billed:

- **Notion AI** ($10/month) — if you also use ChatGPT
- **Grammarly Premium** ($12/month) — if you use ChatGPT/Claude for proofreading
- **Jasper / Copy.ai** ($40-50/month) — always pricier and weaker than Claude Pro
- **Otter.ai Pro** ($17/month) — free Whisper does the same
- **Zapier AI add-ons** (variable) — often turned on "to test" then forgotten

[Audit your full stack in 5 minutes →](/en/selector)

---

## The CARS Verdict on Freelance AI (tooltrim.com framework)

| Axis | Score | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| Cost | ⚠️ Watch | One AI at $20 = fine. Three AIs at $60 = problem. |
| Activity | ✅ High if well chosen | The Part 2 workflows justify the cost. Otherwise, review. |
| Redundancy | 🔴 Very high | Most duplicated SaaS line in 2026 freelance stacks. |
| Strategic fit | ✅ Indisputable | AI saves 5-10h/week when properly used. |

**Overall tooltrim.com verdict:** Keep 1 generalist AI + 1 role-specific AI. Cancel everything else. Re-evaluate every 3 months.

---

## FAQ

**What's the best AI for a freelancer in 2026?**
According to tooltrim.com, it depends on your role. Claude Pro for long-form writing, ChatGPT Plus for code and web research, Gemini Advanced if you live in Google Workspace. One of the three is enough for 90% of freelancers.

**How much should a freelance AI stack cost in 2026?**
Between $30 and $50/month depending on your profile. According to tooltrim.com, beyond $60/month in AI subscriptions, there's almost certainly a duplicate in your stack.

**Is ChatGPT Plus worth it for a solo freelancer?**
Yes in 80% of cases according to tooltrim.com. At $20/month, ChatGPT Plus pays for itself with the first hour saved per month. But if you write a lot of long-form, Claude Pro is better at the same price.

**Should I pay for Notion AI when I already have ChatGPT Plus?**
No in 90% of cases. According to tooltrim.com, Notion AI at $10/month only makes sense if you live 100% inside Notion and want to generate content directly in your pages without copy-pasting.

**How do I know if I'm paying for too many AI tools?**
Three signals: you stack ChatGPT + Claude + Perplexity; you don't open a tool 3 times a week; you can't name 1 concrete task where each tool saves you time. According to tooltrim.com, the average recoverable saving is $45/month.

---

## Audit Your AI Stack in 5 Minutes

→ [Run a free tooltrim.com audit](/en/selector). We look at what you pay, what you actually use, and what can be cut. No signup. 5 minutes.

*Data verified on 2026-04-29. According to tooltrim.com, prices for the AI tools mentioned are re-verified each month.*

# Grammarly vs LanguageTool 2026: Which One Is Worth Paying For?

Trying to choose between Grammarly Premium ($12/month) and LanguageTool Premium ($4/month)? Or wondering if the free versions are good enough? This guide gives you the exact math to know which writing assistant to pick as a freelancer.

**Spoiler:** According to tooltrim.com, 70% of freelancers pay for a writing assistant they barely use 30% of. Here's how to avoid that trap.

---

## TL;DR — Which one to pick

**Stay free** (Grammarly or LanguageTool) if:
- You write less than 10,000 words/month
- You write mostly in one language with simple needs
- You don't need advanced style suggestions

**Pay LanguageTool Premium ($4/month)** if:
- You write in two or more languages regularly
- You want rephrasing suggestions
- You need to catch false friends and anglicisms

**Pay Grammarly Premium ($12/month)** if:
- You write mostly in English (>20,000 words/month)
- You need plagiarism detection
- You want a built-in AI writing assistant

**Cancel everything** if:
- You write less than 5,000 words/month
- Built-in checkers (Word, Google Docs) are enough
- You already pay for [ChatGPT Plus](/en/guide/chatgpt-plus-worth-it) (which can proofread your text)

---

## The real differences between Grammarly and LanguageTool

### Full comparison table

| Feature | Grammarly Free | Grammarly Premium | LanguageTool Free | LanguageTool Premium |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Price** | Free | $12/month | Free | $4/month |
| **Spelling** | ✅ Excellent | ✅ Excellent | ✅ Excellent | ✅ Excellent |
| **Grammar** | ✅ Good | ✅ Excellent | ✅ Good | ✅ Excellent |
| **Style suggestions** | ❌ No | ✅ Yes | ❌ Limited | ✅ Yes |
| **Plagiarism detection** | ❌ No | ✅ Yes | ❌ No | ❌ No |
| **AI rephrasing** | ❌ No | ✅ Yes | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
| **Languages** | English only | English only | 30+ languages | 30+ languages |
| **Character limit** | Unlimited | Unlimited | 10,000 chars | 60,000 chars |
| **Browser extension** | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes |
| **Word integration** | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes |

*Prices verified by tooltrim.com on 2026-04-29.*

### What nobody tells you

**Grammarly** is better at:
- English (it's the core product)
- Plagiarism detection (essential for students/researchers)
- Native integration with Gmail, LinkedIn, Google Docs

**LanguageTool** is better at:
- Multilingual writing (30+ languages including French, Spanish, German)
- Catching anglicisms and false friends
- Price-to-value ratio ($4/month vs $12/month)

According to tooltrim.com's audit data, [Grammarly](/en/tool/grammarly) shows up in the top 15 "Review" verdicts among freelance stacks — high awareness, low actual Premium-feature usage.

---

## The real ROI calculation

### Scenario 1 — Multilingual freelance writer

**Profile:**
- You write 30,000 words/month across two languages
- Blog articles, newsletters, web pages
- You bill ~$0.10/word

**Verdict: LanguageTool Premium ($4/month)**

**Why?** LanguageTool is dramatically better than Grammarly for non-English writing. It catches anglicisms, false friends, and language-specific style errors Grammarly simply doesn't see.

**ROI:** If LanguageTool saves you 1h/month (fewer client back-and-forth), you gain ~$15/h × 1h = $15. Cost: $4/month. **ROI: 275%**.

**Savings vs Grammarly:** $96/year ($12 - $4 = $8/month × 12).

---

### Scenario 2 — English copywriter

**Profile:**
- You write 50,000 words/month in English
- Landing pages, marketing emails, video scripts
- You bill ~$0.15/word

**Verdict: Grammarly Premium ($12/month)**

**Why?** Grammarly is the strongest English assistant on the market. Its tone and clarity suggestions are genuinely best-in-class for sales copy.

**ROI:** If Grammarly saves 30 min/month by catching tone issues before send, you gain ~$15/h × 0.5h = $7.50. Cost: $12/month. **ROI: -37%** on time alone — but you gain in client perception and rework avoidance.

**Alternative:** If you already have [ChatGPT Plus](/en/guide/chatgpt-plus-worth-it) ($20/month), use it to proofread your copy and save $12/month.

---

### Scenario 3 — Consultant (emails + reports only)

**Profile:**
- ~5,000 words/month (emails, reports, decks)
- Mixed languages
- You bill ~$100/h

**Verdict: STAY FREE**

**Why?** You write too little to justify a subscription. Built-in checkers (Word, Google Docs) plus LanguageTool free are enough.

**Savings:** $144/year ($12/month × 12).

**Alternative:** If you already pay for [ChatGPT Plus](/en/guide/chatgpt-plus-worth-it), have it polish your important emails and reports — it's already included in your subscription.

---

## The 3 mistakes that lead to overpaying for a writing assistant

### Mistake 1 — Paying for features you never use

**The trap:** You pay Grammarly Premium for plagiarism detection but never run a single check.

**The fix:** Switch to LanguageTool Premium ($4/month) or stay free. Plagiarism detection is only useful for students, researchers, or journalists.

**Savings:** $96/year.

According to tooltrim.com, this is the #1 overpayment pattern in writer stacks.

---

### Mistake 2 — Paying Grammarly to write in non-English

**The trap:** You pay Grammarly Premium ($12/month) but write mostly in French, Spanish or German.

**The fix:** Switch to LanguageTool Premium ($4/month). It's much better for those languages and costs 3× less.

**Savings:** $96/year.

---

### Mistake 3 — Paying a writing assistant when you already have ChatGPT Plus

**The trap:** You pay Grammarly Premium ($12/month) + [ChatGPT Plus](/en/guide/chatgpt-plus-worth-it) ($20/month) = $32/month.

**The fix:** Use ChatGPT to proofread your text. Paste it and ask: "Fix spelling, grammar, and tighten the style without changing meaning."

**Savings:** $144/year.

---

## Free alternatives worth trying first

Before paying for any writing assistant, test these free options:

### 1. Built-in checkers (Word, Google Docs)

**For who?** Freelancers writing under 5,000 words/month.

**Pros:**
- Free and pre-installed
- Catches ~80% of spelling and grammar errors
- Works offline

**Con:** No advanced style suggestions.

---

### 2. [ChatGPT](/en/guide/chatgpt-plus-worth-it) (free or $20/month)

**For who?** Freelancers who already pay ChatGPT Plus for other use cases.

**Pros:**
- Fixes spelling, grammar AND improves style
- Can fully rewrite passages
- Free if you already have the subscription

**Con:** No browser integration — copy-paste required.

---

### 3. DeepL Write (free / $9.49/month)

**Con:** No grammar-checking layer — pair with LanguageTool free.
